metadata.scope: e_mongolia (315 baronies across k_buryatia, k_gobi, k_otuken, k_shiwei)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_FIC_Mong_Doodonon.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Doodonon) representing the lower Onon River valley; no pre-867 CE written settlement attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Doodonon.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym combining Mongolian dood ('lower') with the hydronym Onon (Onon River). Directional/qualifier compounds are excluded from natural_proper_name.

b_FIC_Mong_Kharbelcheer.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Kharbelcheer) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Kharbelcheer.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym formed from Mongolian khar ('black') and belcheer ('pasture' or 'confluence').

b_FIC_Mong_Shitagol.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Shitagol) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Shitagol.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name combining an uncertain first element (possibly derived from Chita/Shita) with Mongolian gol ('river').

b_Mong_Jiangbian.first_mention_attestation: Generic Chinese-derived CK3 barony name (Jiangbian, 'riverside') in the Onon region; no pre-867 CE written attestation at this site.
b_Mong_Jiangbian.etymology_analysis: From Mandarin Chinese jiāngbiān ('riverside, riverbank'), used here as a generic geographic label rather than an attested medieval settlement.

b_FIC_Mong_Khanazuun.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Khanazuun) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Khanazuun.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym combining Mongolian khana ('wall, cliff-face') with züün ('east').

b_FIC_Mong_Kurumnuur.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Kurumnuur) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Kurumnuur.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym combining Siberian/Turkic kurum ('scree, rock-stream') with Mongolian nuur ('lake').

b_FIC_Mong_Khanabaruun.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Khanabaruun) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Khanabaruun.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym combining Mongolian khana ('wall, cliff-face') with baruun ('west').

b_FIC_Mong_Kyursugol.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Kyursugol) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Kyursugol.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym combining an uncertain stem kyursu with Mongolian gol ('river').

b_FIC_Mong_Paljigol.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Paljigol) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Paljigol.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym combining palji with Mongolian gol ('river').

b_FIC_Mong_Ingedei.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Ingedei) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Ingedei.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name with Mongolic-style suffixation (-dei), not attested in historical sources.

b_FIC_Mong_Chulereg.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Chulereg) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Chulereg.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name with no documented pre-867 CE historical or geographic attestation.

b_FIC_Mong_Ononum.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Ononum), a Latinized/synthetic derivative of the Onon River name; no pre-867 CE written settlement attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Ononum.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 name attaching a Latinate -um suffix to the Onon River hydronym.

b_FIC_Mong_Orgilalkham.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Orgilalkham) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Orgilalkham.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 compound from Mongolian orgil ('peak, summit') and alkham ('step').

b_FIC_Mong_Ulajagol.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Ulajagol) with no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Ulajagol.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 toponym combining ulaja with Mongolian gol ('river').

b_kada_MON.first_mention_attestation: Ust-Kada village in Kuytunsky District, Irkutsk Oblast was founded in 1853 CE by peasants from Uyan; named after the Kada River (tributary of the Oka).
b_kada_MON.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Kada River (a tributary of the Oka in Irkutsk Oblast), which gave its name to the 19th-century Russian settlements Ust-Kada (1853) and Novaya Kada (1900).

b_alyaty.first_mention_attestation: Rural locality (village) and lake in Alarsky District, Irkutsk Oblast; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_alyaty.etymology_analysis: Toponym in Alarsky District, Irkutsk Oblast shared by the village of Alyaty and Lake Alyaty at the foot of the Eastern Sayan Mountains.

b_kurkat.first_mention_attestation: Rural locality (village) in Alarsky District, Irkutsk Oblast; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_kurkat.etymology_analysis: Village in Alarsky District, Irkutsk Oblast, located 31 km from Kutulik; of local Buryat origin with no pre-867 CE documentary record.

b_kitoi.first_mention_attestation: Kitoy River (a left tributary of the Angara in Buryatia and Irkutsk Oblast) and adjacent settlement near Angarsk (founded 1948); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kitoi.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for the 316 km Kitoy River (Buryat: Khuti), a left tributary of the Angara flowing past modern Angarsk.

b_noty.first_mention_attestation: Noty River and Lake Noty in Alarsky District, Irkutsk Oblast; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_noty.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Noty River (which receives the Kutulik stream before joining the Angara) and Lake Noty in Alarsky District, Irkutsk Oblast.

b_olkha.first_mention_attestation: Olkha village in Shelekhovsky District, Irkutsk Oblast was founded in the early 18th century (c. 1700 CE) on the Olkha River, a right tributary of the Irkut.
b_olkha.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 84 km Olkha River, a right tributary of the Irkut, which gave its name to the early 18th-century village of Olkha near Shelekhov.

b_kymyl_tey.first_mention_attestation: Kimiltei (Kymyltey) River (left tributary of the Oka) and village in Ziminsky District, Irkutsk Oblast; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kymyl_tey.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Kimiltei River in Ziminsky District, Irkutsk Oblast, which gave its name to Kimiltei village; likely Buryat or Evenki in origin with the Mongolic suffix -tei.

b_angaragiin_degee.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 Mongolic-translated toponym referencing the Angara River; no pre-867 CE written settlement attestation.
b_angaragiin_degee.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'bend/hook of the Angara'; excluded from natural_proper_name as a compound with a generic topographic noun.

b_zima_MON.first_mention_attestation: The village of Staraya Zima on the site of the modern town of Zima (Irkutsk Oblast) was established in 1743 CE at the confluence of the Zima and Oka rivers.

morphemes.translation: Zima River (reinterpreted in Russian as zima, 'winter')

b_zima_MON.etymology_analysis: Named after the Zima River (a tributary of the Oka), adapted from Buryat Zeme and folk-etymologized in Russian as zima ('winter').

b_okangara.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 portmanteau of the Oka and Angara rivers; no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_okangara.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 blend combining the names of the Oka and Angara rivers.

b_bisha_MON.first_mention_attestation: Bisha River, a tributary of the Angara in Irkutsk Oblast; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_bisha_MON.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Bisha River, a small tributary of the Angara in Irkutsk Oblast.

b_mori_kliringiin.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 toponym ('horse clearing'); no real-world pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_mori_kliringiin.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 compound combining Mongolian mori ('horse') with a loan-calque of 'clearing' plus the Mongolian genitive suffix -iin.

b_kirenga.first_mention_attestation: The Kirenga River (right tributary of the Lena in Irkutsk Oblast) enters written records with the Russian conquest of Siberia (Kirensk founded at its mouth in 1630 CE).
b_kirenga.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of Evenki origin for the 746 km Kirenga River, a major right tributary of the Lena.

b_cherskogo.first_mention_attestation: Named in the late 19th century (post-1870s) after Polish-Russian geologist Jan Czerski (Ivan Chersky, 1845–1892), who explored the Baikal Range.
b_cherskogo.eponym_details: Named after Polish-Russian geologist and explorer Jan Czerski (Ivan Chersky, 1845–1892), who surveyed Lake Baikal and the Baikal Mountains in the 1870s–1880s.
b_cherskogo.etymology_analysis: Russian genitive form of the surname of Jan Czerski (1845–1892), applied to Mount Chersky (Gora Cherskogo), the highest peak of the Baikal Range.

b_baigalan_chaya.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 compound referencing Lake Baikal and the Chaya River (a Lena tributary in Buryatia and Irkutsk Oblast); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_baigalan_chaya.etymology_analysis: Compound toponym pairing Buryat Baigal ('Baikal') with the hydronym Chaya (a 353 km tributary of the Lena).

b_nogoon_naluu.first_mention_attestation: Descriptive Mongolian toponym ('green slope') with no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_nogoon_naluu.etymology_analysis: Generic Mongolian descriptive compound meaning 'green slope'.

b_daoroouul.first_mention_attestation: Descriptive Mongolic compound ('lower mountain'); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_daoroouul.etymology_analysis: Generic directional/topographic compound meaning 'lower mountain' or 'below the mountain'.

b_khilgazar.first_mention_attestation: Descriptive Mongolian compound ('border land'); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_khilgazar.etymology_analysis: Generic Mongolian common-noun compound meaning 'borderland, frontier'.

b_khuldursgal.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 Mongolian compound; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_khuldursgal.etymology_analysis: Synthetic Mongolian compound from khöl ('foot/base') and dursgal ('memorial').

b_chuya.first_mention_attestation: Chuya River, a 512 km right tributary of the Lena in Buryatia and Irkutsk Oblast; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_chuya.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Chuya River (also Big Chuya), a major tributary of the Lena flowing through northern Buryatia and Irkutsk Oblast.

b_alsholoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested Buryat/CK3 barony name in the Bargujin-Chuya region; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_alsholoi.etymology_analysis: Local Buryat-style toponym in the Bargujin-Chuya basin with no documented pre-867 CE historical attestation.

b_chuulunuruu.first_mention_attestation: Descriptive Mongolian compound ('stone slope') with no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_chuulunuruu.etymology_analysis: Generic Mongolian descriptive compound meaning 'rocky slope/descent'.

b_chonoshud.first_mention_attestation: Mongolian toponym/clan-associated name ('wolf tooth'); no pre-867 CE written settlement attestation.
b_chonoshud.etymology_analysis: Mongolian compound literally meaning 'wolf tooth', possibly evoking the Chonos (wolf) clan of the Baikal/Buryat region.

b_karaoi.first_mention_attestation: Descriptive Turkic-Mongolic compound ('black forest/grove'); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_karaoi.etymology_analysis: Generic descriptive compound combining Turkic kara ('black') and Mongolian oi ('forest').

b_kotera.first_mention_attestation: Kotera River, a 245 km tributary of the Upper Angara in Buryatia; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kotera.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 245 km Kotera River, the largest tributary of the Upper Angara in northern Buryatia.

b_gants_khondii.first_mention_attestation: Descriptive Mongolian compound ('single/lone valley'); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_gants_khondii.etymology_analysis: Generic Mongolian descriptive compound meaning 'lone valley'.

b_mamakhondii.first_mention_attestation: Compound naming the valley of the Mama River (a left tributary of the Vitim in Buryatia and Irkutsk Oblast); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_mamakhondii.etymology_analysis: Compound combining the Evenki hydronym Mama (a major tributary of the Vitim) with Mongolian khöndii ('valley').

b_shugel_ondor.first_mention_attestation: Descriptive compound with Mongolian öndör ('height'); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_shugel_ondor.etymology_analysis: Compound combining an uncertain stem shugel with Mongolian öndör ('height, highland').

b_vitim.first_mention_attestation: Vitim (at the confluence of the Vitim and Lena rivers) was first mentioned in 17th-century Russian sources (1621 CE) as a winter fort and trading post, named after the Vitim River.
b_vitim.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the major Vitim River (tributary of the Lena), which gave its name to the 17th-century Russian winter fort of Vitim.

b_vitimkhad.first_mention_attestation: Compound naming a rock/cliff on the Vitim River; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_vitimkhad.etymology_analysis: Compound combining the Vitim River hydronym with Mongolian khad ('rock, cliff').

b_karamuya.first_mention_attestation: Qualifier compound referencing the Muya River (a left tributary of the Vitim in Buryatia); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_karamuya.etymology_analysis: Qualifier compound combining Turkic kara ('black') with the hydronym Muya (a 365 km tributary of the Vitim in Buryatia).

b_anja_TUV.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrography (State Water Register) as the Anzha River (Анжа), a left tributary of the Kan in Krasnoyarsk Krai.
b_anja_TUV.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Ket hydronym *Anzas* (*an* 'mother' + *zas/səs* 'river'), adapted into Russian as *Anzha* (Анжа) and localized in-game as *Anje (Anja)*.

b_tofa_nuruud.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Tofalar (Tofa) people and Tofalaria region in the Eastern Sayan were first documented by Russian explorers in the 17th century.
b_tofa_nuruud.etymology_analysis: Mongolian compound combining the Turkic ethnonym *Tofa* (Tofalar, traditionally 'people of the deer') with *nuruud* ('mountain ridges'), referring to the Eastern Sayan homeland of the Tofalar.

b_kizir.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Kizir River (Кизир) in Krasnoyarsk Krai is documented in post-17th-century Russian Siberian cartography and the State Water Register.
b_kizir.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 300-km right tributary of the Kazyr River in the Eastern Sayan Mountains (Krasnoyarsk Krai), of indigenous South Siberian (Turkic or Yeniseian/Samoyedic) substrate origin.

b_tuba_TUV.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Tuba River (Туба) in the Minusinsk Hollow is documented in Russian sources from the 17th–18th centuries onward.
b_tuba_TUV.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Tuba River, formed by the confluence of the Kazyr and Amyl rivers in Krasnoyarsk Krai; linked to the historical Tubin (Tuba) Yenisei Kyrgyz / Samoyedic-Turkic subgroup.

b_shina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Shinda River (Шинда), a right tributary of the Kizir in Kuraginsky District, is documented in modern Russian hydrography.
b_shina.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 152-km Shinda River (Russian: Шинда, abbreviated in CK3 as *b_shina*), a right tributary of the Kizir in Krasnoyarsk Krai.

b_tiberkul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Lake Tiberkul (Тиберкуль) in Kuraginsky District is documented in modern Russian geography and became widely known after 1991.
b_tiberkul.etymology_analysis: South Siberian Turkic hydronym for Lake Tiberkul in Krasnoyarsk Krai, composed of *tiber/temir* (variously interpreted as 'heavenly' or 'iron') and *kul/köl* ('lake').

b_bolsho_kyzylkul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Lake Bolshoy Kyzylkul (Большой Кызылкуль) in the Minusinsk Depression is documented in modern Russian geography.
b_bolsho_kyzylkul.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Russian-Turkic hydronym combining Russian *bolshoy* ('great/large', distinguishing it from Maly Kyzylkul) with Turkic *kyzyl* ('red') + *kul/köl* ('lake'); localized in-game as *Kyzylkul*.

b_amyl.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Amyl River (Амыл) in Karatuzsky District is documented in Russian Siberian cartography and the State Water Register.
b_amyl.etymology_analysis: Indigenous South Siberian hydronym of the Amyl River, which joins the Kazyr to form the Tuba River in southern Krasnoyarsk Krai.

b_borus.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Borus Ridge (хребет Борус) in the Western Sayan is documented in modern Russian geography and Shushensky Bor National Park.
b_borus.etymology_analysis: Oronym of the five-peaked Borus massif in the Western Sayan Mountains (Krasnoyarsk Krai), of South Siberian Turkic (Khakas) origin.

b_kop_golyn.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; appears to be a game-generated Turkic-Mongolian compound name for the Minusinsk/Kyzylkul area.
b_kop_golyn.etymology_analysis: Compound combining Turkic *köp* ('many') or *kök* with Mongolian *gol-yn* ('of the river'), functioning as a descriptive/synthetic barony name.

b_bratsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1631 CE as Bratsky Ostrog (Братский острог) by Cossack ataman Maxim Perfilyev on the Angara River; localized in-game as Bûra-in-Buryatje (Bura).
b_bratsk.etymology_analysis: Russian *Bratsk* derives from *Bratsky ostrog* (1631), named after the local Buryat population (*bratskiye lyudi*); the in-game form *Bûra-in-Buryatje (Bura)* is a synthetic Buryat-style localization.

b_khereeoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; synthetic or minor Mongolian descriptive toponym ('Raven Forest') used as an unoccupied barony in c_bratsk.
b_khereeoi.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive compound *kheree oi* ('Raven Forest'), a generic common-noun topographic label rather than an established historical settlement.

b_tsasengiin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; synthetic Mongolian-derived barony name in c_bratsk.
b_tsasengiin.etymology_analysis: Derived from Mongolian *tsasan* ('snow') with genitive suffix *-giin* ('of snow / snowy'), used as a synthetic unoccupied barony name.

b_bugyntalbar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Mongolian descriptive compound ('Deer Plain') used as an unoccupied barony in c_bratsk.
b_bugyntalbar.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive compound *bugyn talbar* ('Deer Plain / Field'), a generic common-noun label.

b_chuna.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Chuna River (Russian: Чуна, upper course Uda / Mongolian: Үд, Üd) is documented from the 17th-century Russian expansion into Siberia.
b_chuna.etymology_analysis: Named after the 1,203-km Chuna River (upper course known as the Uda, Mongolian *Üd*, localized in-game as *Üt (Üd)*) in Irkutsk Oblast and Krasnoyarsk Krai.

b_moson_kholtos.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Mongolian descriptive compound ('Ice Crust / Bark') used as an unoccupied barony in c_chuna.
b_moson_kholtos.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive compound *mösön kholtos* ('ice crust / icy bark'), a generic common-noun label.

b_tsartsanmod.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Mongolian descriptive compound ('Frozen Tree') used as an unoccupied barony in c_chuna.
b_tsartsanmod.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive compound *tsartsan mod* ('frozen tree / wood'), a generic common-noun label.

b_biryusa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Biryusa River (Бирюса) in Irkutsk Oblast and Krasnoyarsk Krai is documented from the 17th-century Russian Siberian period.
b_biryusa.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 1,012-km Biryusa River, which joins the Chuna to form the Taseyeva River; linked to South Siberian (Ket/Samoyedic or Turkic) substrate nomenclature.

b_kaduy.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Kaduy (Кадуй) in Nizhneudinsky District, Irkutsk Oblast, is documented as a modern village and railway station; localized in-game as Tulun.
b_kaduy.etymology_analysis: Siberian toponym for the village and station of Kaduy in Nizhneudinsky District, Irkutsk Oblast (localized in-game to the county seat name *Tulun*).

b_tulun.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the second half of the 18th century (c. 1735–1760s) as a village in the Iya River valley, Irkutsk Oblast.
b_tulun.etymology_analysis: Town in Irkutsk Oblast on the Iya River, founded in the 18th century; the name is commonly derived from Buryat/Turkic *tulun* ('leather sack' or 'river bend').

b_kirei.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Kirei River (Кирей), a right tributary of the Iya in Irkutsk Oblast, is documented in modern Russian hydrography.
b_kirei.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Kirei (Bolshoy Kirei) River, a major right tributary of the Iya River in the Eastern Sayan foothills of Irkutsk Oblast.

b_bargajan.first_mention_attestation: The toponym Bargujin-Töküm is first attested c. 1240 CE in The Secret History of the Mongols; the Russian ostrog of Barguzin was founded in 1648 CE by Ivan Galkin.
b_bargajan.etymology_analysis: Buryat *Bargajan* (Russian *Barguzin*), naming the 480-km river and valley east of Lake Baikal; associated with the historical Bargut/Barga people and attested as *Bargujin-Töküm* in *The Secret History of the Mongols* (c. 1240 CE).

b_khilem_khamar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Buryat-Mongolian topographic compound ('Sturgeon Cape') in the Barguzin/Baikal region.
b_khilem_khamar.etymology_analysis: Buryat/Mongolian descriptive compound *khilem khamar* ('Sturgeon Cape/Headland'), a generic common-noun topographic label.

b_frolikha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Lake Frolikha (Фролиха) in northern Buryatia is documented in post-17th-century Russian Siberian geography.
b_frolikha.etymology_analysis: Russian hydronym for glacial Lake Frolikha (and the Frolikha River) near northern Lake Baikal; local Russian legend attributes the name to a 17th–18th-century hunter named Frol (Earlier Evenki name: *Nerunda*).

b_kotokel.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Lake Kotokel (Котокель) and the nearby settlement in Pribaykalsky District, Buryatia, are documented from the Russian Siberian period.
b_kotokel.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of Lake Kotokel on the eastern shore of Lake Baikal in Buryatia (and the modern settlement of Kotokel on its southwestern shore), of indigenous Evenki/Buryat origin.

b_kabans.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1678 CE as a Russian fort/settlement (Кабанск) on the Selenga River in Buryatia.
b_kabans.etymology_analysis: Russian *Kabansk* (Buryat: *Khabaan*), founded in 1678 CE as one of the earliest Russian settlements in Transbaikalia, named from Russian *kaban* ('wild boar').

b_itantsa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Itantsa River (Итанца) in Pribaykalsky District, Buryatia, is documented from the 17th-century Russian Siberian period.
b_itantsa.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Itantsa River, a major tributary of the Selenga in Pribaykalsky District, Buryatia.

b_muya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Muya River (Муя), a left tributary of the Vitim in Buryatia, is documented in post-17th-century Russian Siberian geography.
b_muya.etymology_analysis: Evenki/Tungusic hydronym of the 365-km Muya River in northern Buryatia (localized in-game as *Muye (Muya)*).

b_jergin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Dzherginsky (Джергинский) derives from the Dzherga River in the upper Barguzin valley, documented in modern Russian geography.
b_jergin.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Dzherga River in Kurumkansky District, Buryatia, which gives its name to the Dzherginsky Nature Reserve (established 1992).

b_vitimkan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Vitimkan River (Витимкан), western headwater of the Vitim in Buryatia, is documented in modern Russian hydrography.
b_vitimkan.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Vitimkan River, the western source stream of the Vitim River in Buryatia, formed from *Vitim* + diminutive *-kan*.

b_yera.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Yeravna (Еравна, Buryat: Ярууна, Yaruuna) in eastern Buryatia is documented from the 17th-century Russian Siberian period.
b_yera.etymology_analysis: Shortened from *Yeravna* (Buryat: *Yaruuna*, localized in-game as *Jere (Yera)*), referring to the Yeravna-Khorga lake system and Yeravninsky District in eastern Buryatia.

b_shilmuustoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Buryat/Mongolian descriptive term ('having conifers / needles') used as an unoccupied barony in c_yera.
b_shilmuustoi.etymology_analysis: Mongolian/Buryat descriptive adjective *shilmüüstei* ('coniferous / having pine needles'), a generic common-noun label.

b_zuunbaykal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; directional compound ('East Baikal') used as an unoccupied barony in c_yera.
b_zuunbaykal.etymology_analysis: Mongolian directional compound *züün* ('east') + *Baykal* ('Lake Baikal'), i.e., 'East Baikal / Transbaikalia', excluded from natural proper names due to the directional qualifier.

b_karauda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Turkic-Mongolian hydronymic compound ('Black Uda') in the Eastern Sayan, localized in-game as Karaude (Karauda).
b_karauda.etymology_analysis: Compound of Turkic *kara* ('black') + *Uda* (the upper Chuna River in the Eastern Sayan), excluded from natural proper names due to the color qualifier.

b_iya_TUV.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Iya River (Ия) in Irkutsk Oblast is documented from the Russian Siberian period.
b_iya_TUV.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 484-km Iya River, which rises in the Eastern Sayan Mountains and flows past Tulun into the Okinsky Bay of the Bratsk Reservoir.

b_doloon_nuur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Mongolian descriptive compound ('Seven Lakes') used as an unoccupied barony in c_karauda.
b_doloon_nuur.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive numeral compound *doloon nuur* ('Seven Lakes'), a generic common-noun topographic label.

b_kropot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; the Kropotkin Range in the Eastern Sayan was explored by Peter Kropotkin in 1865 and subsequently named in his honor.
b_kropot.eponym_details: Named after Russian geographer, geologist, and anarchist Peter Alekseevich Kropotkin (1842–1921), who explored the Eastern Sayan Mountains in 1865.
b_kropot.etymology_analysis: Abbreviated in CK3 as *Kropot* from the *Kropotkin Range* (Russian: хребет Кропоткина) in the Eastern Sayan, named after 19th-century Russian scientist Peter Kropotkin (1842–1921).

b_urik.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; the Urik River (Урик) in Buryatia and Irkutsk Oblast is documented from the 17th century, with the rural locality of Urik founded in 1673 CE.
b_urik.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 210-km Urik River, a right tributary of the Belaya River flowing from the Eastern Sayan in Buryatia and Irkutsk Oblast.

b_setgel_uul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Mongolian descriptive compound ('Soul / Mind Mountain') used as an unoccupied barony in c_kropot.
b_setgel_uul.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive compound *setgel uul* ('Soul/Mind Mountain'), a generic common-noun label.

b_monkh_saridag.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Mönkh Saridag (Munku-Sardyk), the highest peak of the Sayan Mountains, is documented in modern Russian and Mongolian geography.
b_monkh_saridag.etymology_analysis: Mongolian/Buryat *Mönkh Saridag* (Buryat: *Münkhe Har'dag*, Russian: *Munku-Sardyk*, localized in-game as *Mönchsaridach*), meaning 'eternal snow-capped peak'.

b_khurel_uul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Mongolian descriptive compound ('Bronze Mountain') used as an unoccupied barony in c_monkh_saridag.
b_khurel_uul.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive compound *khürel uul* ('Bronze Mountain'), a generic common-noun label.

b_shityy.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Bolshoy and Maly Shityy rivers (Бол. / Мал. Шитый), tributaries of the upper Iya in the Eastern Sayan, are documented in modern Russian hydrography.
b_shityy.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Bolshoy and Maly Shityy rivers, upper tributaries of the Iya River in the Eastern Sayan (localized in-game as *Schitî (Shityy)*).

b_tsagaan_kropot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; synthetic CK3 compound combining Mongolian 'white' with the post-1865 Kropotkin Range name.
b_tsagaan_kropot.eponym_details: Derived from the Kropotkin Range (Eastern Sayan), named after Russian geographer and anarchist Peter Kropotkin (1842–1921).
b_tsagaan_kropot.etymology_analysis: Synthetic Mongolian-Russian compound combining *tsagaan* ('white') with *Kropot* (shortened from the Kropotkin Range, named after Peter Kropotkin, 1842–1921).

b_dibi_TUV.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Dibi River (Диби), a left tributary of the Oka in Okinsky District, Buryatia, is documented in modern Russian hydrography.
b_dibi_TUV.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 100-km Dibi River (Russian: Диби) in Okinsky District, Buryatia, rising in the Bolshoy Sayan and flowing into the Oka River.

b_fic_mong_dutulunels.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 fictional barony (b_fic_mong_dutulunels); unattested in historical sources <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_dutulunels.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony (*b_fic_mong_dutulunels*) created for *d_em_tataria* (*c_em_dutulun*), not corresponding to a documented historical settlement <= 867 CE.

b_fic_mong_semkut.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_semkut) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_semkut.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 placeholder name (b_fic_mong_*) created for the unoccupied barony in c_em_dutulun (d_em_tataria).

b_fic_mong_tarkilechi.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_tarkilechi) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_tarkilechi.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 placeholder name (b_fic_mong_*) created for the unoccupied barony in c_em_dutulun (d_em_tataria).

b_fic_mong_elskhol.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_elskhol, in-game localized as Gobidade / Gobidada) with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_elskhol.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_gobidada, localized in-game as Gobidade (Gobidada). The key combines Mongolic-style elements els ('sand') and khol.

b_fic_mong_chusolalin.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_chusolalin) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_chusolalin.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_gobidada, formed with the Manchu toponymic element alin ('mountain').

b_fic_mong_payenula.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_payenula) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_payenula.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_gobidada, modeled on Mongolic/Manchu toponymic elements bayan ('rich') and uul ('mountain') or ula ('river').

b_fic_mong_olokuialin.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_olokuialin) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_olokuialin.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_gobidada, formed with the Manchu toponymic element alin ('mountain').

b_fic_mong_karepuri.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_karepuri, in-game localized as Cherulendade / Kherulendada) with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_karepuri.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_kherulendada, localized in-game as Cherulendade (Kherulendada).

b_fic_mong_kukuchol.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_kukuchol) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_kukuchol.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_kherulendada, modeled on Mongolic kükü choluu ('blue stone').

b_fic_mong_hinkanalin.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_hinkanalin) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_hinkanalin.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_kherulendada, combining Khingan (Hinkan) with Manchu alin ('mountain').

b_mong_zhen.first_mention_attestation: Generic CK3 barony (b_mong_zhen, in-game Dschen / Zhen) representing a Chinese-style garrison town (zhen) without a specific <= 867 CE settlement attestation.
b_mong_zhen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Chinese zhèn (鎮, 'garrison town / township'), used in CK3 for c_em_zhen in d_em_tataria.

b_fic_mong_ulantolgod.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_ulantolgod) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_ulantolgod.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_zhen, modeled on Mongolian ulaan tolgod ('red hills').

b_fic_mong_ulyntsana.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_ulyntsana) in e_mongolia with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_ulyntsana.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 placeholder name (b_fic_mong_*) created for the unoccupied barony in c_em_zhen (d_em_tataria).

b_fic_mong_herulun.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_fic_mong_herulun) named after the Kherlen (Herulun) River, with no specific <= 867 CE settlement attestation.
b_fic_mong_herulun.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_*) in c_em_zhen, echoing the Mongolic name of the Kherlen (Herulun) River.

b_abakan.first_mention_attestation: Abakansky ostrog (fort) was built at the mouth of the Abakan River in 1675 CE; the selo of Ust-Abakanskoye was founded in the 1780s and granted town status as Abakan in 1931.
b_abakan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Abakan River; in Khakas and Turkic folk etymology, interpreted as 'bear's blood' (aba-qan) or associated with the legendary hero Aba Khan.

b_ulugkol.first_mention_attestation: Lake Ulug-Kol is a bitter-salty steppe lake in Khakassia (now part of the Khakassia Nature Reserve), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_sosno.first_mention_attestation: Modern Russian-derived toponym (Sosno / Sosnovka) in the Minusinsk-Abakan basin with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sosno.etymology_analysis: Derived from Russian sosna ('pine tree'), a common Siberian settlement/locality name.

b_jerjul.first_mention_attestation: Zherzhul (Dzherzhul) is a river and small settlement in Mansky District, Krasnoyarsk Krai, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_jerjul.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Zherzhul River (a tributary of the Mana in Krasnoyarsk Krai), likely of Yeniseian or Samoyedic substrate origin.

b_argyjek.first_mention_attestation: Argyzhek is a river/locality in the southern Krasnoyarsk Krai / Khakassia region with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_argyjek.etymology_analysis: Siberian hydronym in the Krasnoyarsk/Khakassia basin.

b_sisim.first_mention_attestation: The Sisim River is a right tributary of the Yenisei in southern Krasnoyarsk Krai (known for 19th-century gold placers), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sisim.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Sisim River in the Eastern Sayan foothills of Krasnoyarsk Krai, of pre-Russian Yeniseian/Sayan substrate origin.

b_julym.first_mention_attestation: The Chulym River (in-game Ôver-Tschulîm / Julym) in Khakassia and Krasnoyarsk Krai is documented from Russian Siberian exploration in the 17th century (Chulym town founded 1762), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_julym.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Chulym River (a major right tributary of the Ob formed by the Bely Iyus and Cherny Iyus in Khakassia).

b_yezagash.first_mention_attestation: The Yezagash River is a left tributary of the Yenisei in Balakhtinsky District, Krasnoyarsk Krai, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_yezagash.etymology_analysis: From Khakas Yzygas, literally meaning 'wagtail', transferred as the hydronym of a left tributary of the Yenisei.

b_uchum.first_mention_attestation: Lake Uchum (and the nearby resort/settlement Ozero Uchum in Uzhursky District, Krasnoyarsk Krai) has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_uchum.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of Lake Uchum in southwestern Krasnoyarsk Krai.

b_gatsuurgazar.first_mention_attestation: Toponym in the Lena/Baikal region (in-game Gatzûrgazar / Gatsuurgazar) with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gatsuurgazar.etymology_analysis: Compound of Mongolian gatsuur ('spruce') and gazar ('land, place').

b_kjoosonoi.first_mention_attestation: Locality in the upper Lena / Buryat-Irkutsk region with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_ilim_MON.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1630 CE on the Ilim River as Ilimsky Ostrog ('Fort Ilim') on the Russian portage route to the Lena River.
b_ilim_MON.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ilim River (a right tributary of the Angara), of Evenki/Tungusic origin; in-game localized as Ilge (Ilga) from the nearby Ilga county.

b_ilga.first_mention_attestation: The Ilga River (a left tributary of the upper Lena in Irkutsk Oblast) has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ilga.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Ilga River, 32nd-longest tributary of the Lena River in Irkutsk Oblast.

b_ivda.first_mention_attestation: The Ivda (Ilda) River is a right tributary of the Ilga River in Irkutsk Oblast, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ivda.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Ivda (Ilda) River, a right tributary of the Ilga in the upper Lena basin.

b_lena.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in Russian exploration accounts of 1620–1623 CE (Demid Pyanda) and documented expeditions of 1628–1632 (Vasily Bugor, Pyotr Beketov).
b_lena.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Evenki name Elyu-Ene ('the Large River'; in-game rendered Eülge from Buryat/Mongolic Zülkhe/Zülge).

b_kutukan_ondort.first_mention_attestation: Kutukan is a river/lake hydronym in the Lena basin of Irkutsk Oblast with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kutukan_ondort.etymology_analysis: Siberian hydronym in the Lena basin (Irkutsk Oblast), likely of Evenki origin.

b_ichikta.first_mention_attestation: The Ichikta River is a left tributary of the Kirenga River in Kazachinsko-Lensky District, Irkutsk Oblast, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ichikta.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Ichikta River in the Kirenga–Lena basin, of Evenki origin.

b_FIC_Mong_Khaldun.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_Khaldun, in-game Chaldun / Khaldun) referencing Burkhan Khaldun, which itself is first attested in The Secret History of the Mongols (c. 1240 CE).
b_FIC_Mong_Khaldun.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_FIC_Mong_*) echoing Burkhan Khaldun in the Khentii Mountains.

b_FIC_Mong_Ononekh.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_FIC_Mong_Ononekh) in c_EM_khaldun with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Ononekh.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_FIC_Mong_*) meaning 'source/headwaters of the Onon River' (Onon ekh).

b_FIC_Mong_Ulaondor.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_FIC_Mong_Ulaondor) in c_EM_khaldun with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Ulaondor.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_FIC_Mong_*) combining Mongolian ulaan ('red') and öndör ('high, height').

b_FIC_Mong_Olongoluud.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony (b_FIC_Mong_Olongoluud) in c_EM_khaldun with no documented historical settlement attestation.
b_FIC_Mong_Olongoluud.etymology_analysis: Fictional CK3 barony name (b_FIC_Mong_*) meaning 'many rivers' (olon gol-uud) in Mongolian.

b_khentii.first_mention_attestation: The Khentii Mountains (in-game Chentî / Khentii) are attested by the Mongolic name Khentii only in post-867 CE sources; the range was earlier known in Han Chinese records as Langjuxu (119 BCE).
b_khentii.etymology_analysis: Mongolian oronym for the Khentii Mountains in northeastern Mongolia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) and Book of Han (Huo Qubing's 119 BCE campaign) (compiled c. 91 BCE, recording 119 BCE campaign)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han general Huo Qubing reached Mount Langjuxu (狼居胥山), identified with the Khentii Mountains, during his 119 BCE campaign against the Xiongnu.

b_tuul_khentii.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Old Turkic Tonyukuk inscription (c. 716 CE) at Bayn Tsokto near the river as Toɣla / Tuɣla, and in Tang dynasty chronicles as Dule (獨樂水).

morphemes.translation: to cross / traverse (or Old Turkic Toɣla)

b_tuul_khentii.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Tuul River in central and northern Mongolia, attested in Old Turkic as Toɣla/Tuɣla in the 8th-century Tonyukuk inscriptions and linked in Mongolian to tuulakh ('to cross/traverse').

b_gorkhii_terelj.first_mention_attestation: Gorkhi-Terelj (stream/valley and national park in Töv Province, Mongolia) has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gorkhii_terelj.etymology_analysis: Compound of Mongolian gorkhi ('brook, stream') and terelj ('rhododendron').

b_burkal.first_mention_attestation: The Burkal River is a tributary of the Menza River in Zabaykalsky Krai, Russia, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_burkal.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Burkal River in the Chikoy–Selenga basin of Transbaikalia.

b_naushki.first_mention_attestation: Naushki was established as Russia's border railway station on the Ulan-Ude–Naushki line of the Trans-Mongolian Railway (station opened 1940 CE).
b_naushki.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation (Naushki) of the local Buryat name Naashkhi, developed into an urban-type settlement around the 1940 border railway station.

b_chikoy_OGR.first_mention_attestation: The Chikoy River (a major right tributary of the Selenga in Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai) is documented from 17th-century Russian expansion, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_chikoy_OGR.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Chikoy River in Transbaikalia.

b_oarkhan_uul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested/variant Mongolic toponym (likely a variant of Darkhan-Uul or Orkhon-Uul in northern Mongolia) with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_oarkhan_uul.etymology_analysis: Mongolic compound with uul ('mountain'), representing a CK3 variant of Darkhan-Uul or Orkhon-Uul in northern Mongolia.

b_ulaanbaatar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1639 CE as the movable yurt monastery Örgöö ('palace-yurt', in-game Örgô), settling permanently at its current site in 1778 and renamed Ulaanbaatar in 1924.
b_ulaanbaatar.etymology_analysis: Originally founded as Örgöö ('palace-yurt', 1639) and later renamed Ulaanbaatar ('Red Hero', 1924).

b_moltsog_els.first_mention_attestation: Moltsog Els is a sand-dune formation in Mongolia (near Hustai National Park / Gobi) with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_moltsog_els.etymology_analysis: Mongolian topographic name combining moltsog ('tassel/tuft') and els ('sand').

b_hustai.first_mention_attestation: The Khustai (Hustai) Mountains in Töv Province, Mongolia (now Hustai National Park), have no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_hustai.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian khustai ('with birch trees'), from khus ('birch') + associative suffix -tai.

b_orkhontuul.first_mention_attestation: Orkhontuul is a modern sum (district) of Selenge Province in northern Mongolia, named after the confluence of the Orkhon and Tuul rivers, with no settlement attestation <= 867 CE.
b_orkhontuul.etymology_analysis: Compound district name combining the Orkhon and Tuul rivers, which meet near Orkhontuul sum in Selenge Province.

b_baibalik.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bay-Balïq in the Old Turkic Shine Usu inscription (759–761 CE), which records that Uyghur Khagan Bayanchur (Moyanchur) ordered Chinese and Sogdian builders to construct the fortified city on the Selenga River around 757–758 CE.
b_baibalik.etymology_analysis: From Old Turkic Bay-Balïq ('rich city'), constructed around 757–758 CE under Uyghur Khagan Bayanchur. In modern Mongolian, the ruins in Khutag-Öndör sum, Bulgan Province are known as Biibulagyn Balgas.

b_namnan_uul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; first documented in modern Mongolian cartographic and conservation records (Namnan Uul Nature Reserve established in 2003).
b_namnan_uul.etymology_analysis: Mongolian oronym referring to the Namnan mountain range in Khutag-Öndör sum, Bulgan Province, northern Mongolia, composed of the proper name Namnan and uul ('mountain').

b_airkhan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; documented in modern Mongolian geographical and ecological surveys.
b_airkhan.etymology_analysis: Mongolian hydronym for Airkhan Lake (Airkhan Nuur), a shallow steppe lake located south of the Eg River in northern Mongolia.

b_karatsagaan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; appears in Crusader Kings III as a compound of Turkic/Mongolic color terms without a documented pre-867 CE settlement.
b_karatsagaan.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Turkic-Mongolic toponymic compound combining Turkic kara ('black') and Mongolian tsagaan ('white'), rendered in-game as Karatschagân.

b_khargal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; documented in modern Mongolian geographical and hydrological records as Lake Khargal in Khövsgöl Province.
b_khargal.etymology_analysis: Mongolian hydronym for Lake Khargal (Khargal Nuur) in northern Mongolia's Khövsgöl Province.

b_jida.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Dzhida River in southern Buryatia was first documented by Russian explorers and cartographers in the 17th–18th centuries.
b_jida.etymology_analysis: Russian Dzhida (Джида), adapted from Buryat Zede (Зэдэ) / Mongolian Zed, a left tributary of the Selenga River in Buryatia, often linked to Mongolic zed ('copper').

b_khokhoo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; appears as a Mongolian toponym (Khökhöö, rendered Chöchô in-game) with no pre-867 CE documentary record.
b_khokhoo.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian khökhöö ('cuckoo'), a common element in Mongolian place names, rendered in-game as Chöchô.

b_erkhel.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; although surrounded by Bronze Age deer stones and khirigsuurs, the name Erkhel Lake is only attested in modern Mongolian records.
b_erkhel.etymology_analysis: Mongolian hydronym for Erkhel Lake (Erkhel Nuur), a saline steppe lake in Alag-Erdene sum, Khövsgöl Province, Mongolia.

b_dayan_deerkhiin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; Dayan Deerkhiin Agui (Dayan Deerkh Cave) and its nearby monastery are documented in later Mongolian shamanic and Buddhist traditions.
b_dayan_deerkhiin.etymology_analysis: Mongolian toponymic genitive form Dayan Deerkhiin ('of Dayan Deerkh'), referring to the sacred Dayan Deerkh Cave in Tsagaan-Üür sum, Khövsgöl Province.

b_selenga.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Seleŋe in the Old Turkic Tonyukuk inscription (c. 720–726 CE), as well as in the Bilge Khagan inscription (735 CE) and Shine Usu inscription (759–761 CE).
b_selenga.etymology_analysis: Recorded in Old Turkic runic inscriptions as Seleŋe; later etymologized either from Mongolian selekh ('to swim') or Evenki sele ('iron') with the possessive suffix -nge.

b_buteeliin_nuruu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; documented in modern Mongolian geographical surveys as the Büteeliin Nuruu mountain range.
b_buteeliin_nuruu.etymology_analysis: Mongolian oronym meaning 'Ridge of Accomplishment/Creation', designating a mountain range in northern Mongolia near the Selenge-Russian border.

b_khamar_daban.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Khamar-Daban mountain range south of Lake Baikal was first documented in post-medieval Russian and Buryat records.
b_khamar_daban.etymology_analysis: From Buryat Khamar-Dabaan (Һамар дабаан), combining khamar ('nose, promontory') and dabaan ('mountain pass').

b_galuut_nuur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; Gusinoye Lake (Buryat: Galuut Nuur) is first documented in 17th–18th century Russian and Buryat records.
b_galuut_nuur.etymology_analysis: Buryat Galuut Nuur (Галуут нуур, 'Goose Lake'), corresponding to Russian Gusinoye Ozero (Гусиное озеро), located in southern Buryatia.

b_arshan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; the mineral spring resort village of Arshan in Tunkinsky District, Buryatia was established in the late 19th to early 20th century (mineral springs publicized in 1894; reserve decreed in 1909).
b_arshan.etymology_analysis: From Buryat arshaan ('healing mineral spring'), itself a borrowing via Mongolic from Sanskrit rasāyana ('elixir').

b_kyngarga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Kyngarga River in Tunkinsky District, Buryatia is documented in modern Russian and Buryat geographical sources (e.g., 1909 Arshan reserve decree).
b_kyngarga.etymology_analysis: Russian Kyngarga, derived from Buryat khengerge ('drum'), referring to the roaring sound of the river's waterfalls in the Eastern Sayan Mountains.

b_dachi_gama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; no pre-867 CE settlement or feature named Dachi Gama is documented in historical records.
b_dachi_gama.etymology_analysis: Obscure or synthetic Crusader Kings III barony name in the Tunka county with no verified pre-867 CE historical or geographical attestation.

b_kuznetsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1618 CE as Kuznetsky ostrog, a Russian Cossack fortress on the Tom River; renamed Novokuznetsk in 1932.
b_kuznetsk.etymology_analysis: From Russian kuznets ('smith, blacksmith'), referring to the iron-smelting skills of the indigenous Shor people ('Kuznetsk Tatars').

b_kuztom.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; synthetic Crusader Kings III portmanteau combining Kuznetsk and the Tom River.
b_kuztom.etymology_analysis: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony name formed by combining the Russian prefix Kuz- (from Kuznetsk/Kuzbas) with Tom (the Tom River).

b_kuzalatau.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; synthetic Crusader Kings III portmanteau derived from the Kuznetsk Alatau mountain range.
b_kuzalatau.etymology_analysis: Synthetic Crusader Kings III contraction of Kuznetsk Alatau (a mountain range in southern Siberia), combining Kuz- with Turkic alatau ('mottled/snow-streaked mountain').

b_kondoma_MON.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Kondoma River in Kemerovo Oblast was first documented in Russian 17th-century Siberian records.
b_kondoma_MON.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for the Kondoma River, a left tributary of the Tom River flowing through Mountain Shoria into Novokuznetsk.

b_mrassu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Mrassu (Mras-Su) River in Mountain Shoria was first documented in Russian 17th-century Siberian records.
b_mrassu.etymology_analysis: From Shor Mras-Su (Russian Mrassu), a left tributary of the Tom River in Kemerovo Oblast, combining the hydronymic base Mras with Turkic su ('water, river').

b_shor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the ethnonym 'Shors' and the regional name 'Gornaya Shoriya' (Mountain Shoria) entered Russian and ethnographic usage in the 19th–20th centuries.
b_shor.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Shor clan name, generalized by 19th-century Russian ethnographers (such as Vasily Radlov) to the Turkic-speaking people and region of Mountain Shoria.

b_abaza.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1856 CE (or 1867 CE) as a settlement around the Abakan ironworks on the Abakan River in Khakassia.
b_abaza.etymology_analysis: Russian syllabic abbreviation of Abakansky Zavod ('Abakan Ironworks'), founded in the mid-19th century.

b_khartomor_uul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; synthetic or unverified Mongolic-style barony name in Crusader Kings III.
b_khartomor_uul.etymology_analysis: Mongolian compound meaning 'Black Iron Mountain' (khar 'black' + tömör 'iron' + uul 'mountain'), used as a Crusader Kings III barony in d_shoria without pre-867 CE attestation.

b_granuul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; synthetic Crusader Kings III barony name in d_shoria.
b_granuul.etymology_analysis: Synthetic Crusader Kings III barony name combining an obscure element gran with Mongolian uul ('mountain').

b_arzhan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by name in written sources before 867 CE; while the Arzhan-1 and Arzhan-2 Saka kurgans date archaeologically to the 9th–7th centuries BCE, the Tuvan toponym Arzhan is only documented in modern times.
b_arzhan.etymology_analysis: From Tuvan arzhaan ('mineral spring'), borrowed via Mongolic from Sanskrit rasāyana ('elixir'). The archaeological site in Tuva is named after the nearby modern settlement.

b_saryg_sep.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; the village of Saryg-Sep in Kaa-Khemsky District, Tuva was founded in 1904 CE.
b_saryg_sep.etymology_analysis: From Tuvan Sarıg-Sep ('yellow river branch'), a rural locality founded in 1904 in Tuva.

b_por_bajin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by name in written sources before 867 CE; tree-ring dating shows the Uyghur palace/fortress on Lake Tere-Khol was built around 777 CE, but its original 8th-century name is unrecorded and 'Por-Bazhyn' is a later Tuvan descriptive name.
b_por_bajin.etymology_analysis: From Tuvan Por-Bazhyng ('clay house'), a later descriptive name given to the 8th-century Uyghur mud-brick island complex on Lake Tere-Khol in southern Tuva.

b_azas.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; Lake Azas (Todzha Lake) and the Azas River in northeastern Tuva are documented in modern Russian and Tuvan geographical sources.
b_azas.etymology_analysis: Tuvan hydronym for Azas Lake (also called Todzha Lake) and the Azas River in the Todzha Basin of northeastern Tuva.

b_eki_khem.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; Tuvan-style compound with no pre-867 CE documentary record.
b_eki_khem.etymology_analysis: Tuvan compound meaning 'good river' (eki 'good' + khem 'river'), used as a barony in d_togina.

b_tapsa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Tapsa River in the Biy-Khem basin of Tuva is documented in modern Russian and Tuvan geographical and geological surveys.
b_tapsa.etymology_analysis: Tuvan hydronym for the Tapsa River, a tributary in the Biy-Khem (Great Yenisei) basin in Tuva.

b_ikh_nogoon.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; Mongolian descriptive toponym with no pre-867 CE documentary record.
b_ikh_nogoon.etymology_analysis: Mongolian descriptive compound meaning 'Great Green' (ikh 'great' + nogoon 'green').

b_ak_altyg_khol.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; documented in modern Tuvan and Russian geographical records.
b_ak_altyg_khol.etymology_analysis: Tuvan hydronym (rendered Ak-Altyg-Khol in-game), combining ak ('white'), attyg ('with horses' or 'named'), and khöl ('lake').

b_bilin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Bilin River, a tributary of the Little Yenisei (Kaa-Khem) in Tuva, is documented in modern Russian and Tuvan geographical sources.
b_bilin.etymology_analysis: Tuvan hydronym for the Bilin River, an upper tributary of the Little Yenisei (Kaa-Khem) in southeastern Tuva.

b_irkutsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1661 CE by Russian Cossacks under Yakov Pokhabov as the Irkutsk ostrog near the confluence of the Irkut and Angara rivers; granted town rights in 1686 CE.
b_irkutsk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Irkut River (Buryat Erkhüü, rendered in-game as Erhû), combined with the Russian toponymic suffix -sk.

b_osa_MON.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the settlement of Osa in Irkutsk Oblast (Ust-Orda Buryat Okrug) was established after the 17th-century Russian expansion into Buryatia.
b_osa_MON.etymology_analysis: Named after the Osa River (Buryat Ooһo), a right tributary of the Angara River in Irkutsk Oblast.

b_KUDA_MON.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Kuda River (a tributary of the Angara in Irkutsk Oblast) is first documented in 17th-century Russian Siberian records.
b_KUDA_MON.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for the Kuda River, a right tributary of the Angara River northeast of Irkutsk inhabited by Western Buryats.

b_olkhon.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; first recorded in written history in 1643 CE when Russian explorer Kurbat Ivanov reached Lake Baikal and Olkhon Island.
b_olkhon.etymology_analysis: Derived from Buryat oikhon ('wooded' or 'little forest') or olkhon ('dry'), referring to the largest island in Lake Baikal.

b_bugulde.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Buguldeika River and village on the western shore of Lake Baikal are first documented in post-17th-century Russian records.
b_bugulde.etymology_analysis: From Buryat Bugulde (Russian Buguldeika), a river flowing into Lake Baikal southwest of Olkhon Island.

b_manzurka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Manzurka River (a tributary of the Lena in Irkutsk Oblast) and nearby village are documented in post-17th-century Russian records.
b_manzurka.etymology_analysis: Russian hydronymic adaptation with suffix -ka from a local Buryat or Evenki river name, designating a left tributary of the upper Lena River in Irkutsk Oblast.

b_ryty.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; Cape Ryty on the northwestern shore of Lake Baikal was named in Russian after the 17th-century Russian arrival at Lake Baikal.
b_ryty.etymology_analysis: From Russian ryty ('dug, furrowed'), referring to the deep mudflow-carved ravines and gullies on the cape's slopes on Lake Baikal's northwest coast.

b_berikul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the toponym Berikul in Siberia is documented only in modern Russian records.
b_berikul.etymology_analysis: Likely from Siberian Turkic böri ('wolf') + köl ('lake'), adapted into Russian as Berikul.

b_chikan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Chikan River and village in Zhigalovsky District, Irkutsk Oblast are documented only in post-17th-century Russian records.
b_chikan.etymology_analysis: Hydronym and settlement name in the upper Lena basin of Irkutsk Oblast, of local Evenki or Buryat origin.

b_chikoy.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Chikoy River (a right tributary of the Selenga) was first documented in 17th-century Russian Siberian records.
b_chikoy.etymology_analysis: Russian Chikoy (Чикой), adapted from Buryat Tsökhe (Цүхэ) or Evenki, designating a major right tributary of the Selenga River.

b_khilok.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources before 867 CE; the Khilok River was first documented in 17th-century Russian Siberian records, and the modern town of Khilok was founded in 1895 CE as a Trans-Siberian Railway station.
b_khilok.etymology_analysis: Russian Khilok (Хилок), adapted from Buryat Khyoolgo (Хёолго) / Mongolian Khilgo, a right tributary of the Selenga River.

b_oungo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrological and geographical surveys (State Water Register, Encyclopedia of Transbaikalia) as a 189 km left tributary of the Khilok River in Zabaykalsky Krai.
b_oungo.etymology_analysis: Hydronym in the Khilok/Selenga basin derived from Evenki Ung ('sending, dispatch'), adapted into Russian as Ungo.

b_ulan_ude.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1666 CE as the Russian Cossack winter settlement and fort of Udinskoye (Удинское) at the confluence of the Uda and Selenga rivers; renamed Verkhneudinsk in 1783 CE and Ulan-Ude in 1934 CE.
b_ulan_ude.etymology_analysis: Compound city name adopted in 1934 CE from Buryat ulaan ('red', Soviet ideological epithet) and Üde (the Uda River, itself linked to Yakut üüt 'milk').

b_altaichei.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; modern rural locality (ulus) in Bichursky District, Republic of Buryatia, documented in modern Russian and Buryat administrative records.
b_altaichei.etymology_analysis: Buryat settlement name (Altasha, Russianized as Altachey) derived from Buryat alta(n) ('gold, golden') with the suffix -sha.

b_khudan_BUR.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian and Buryat geographical surveys as the 252 km Khudan (Kudun) River and valley, a left tributary of the Uda River in Buryatia.
b_khudan_BUR.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Buryat hydronym (Khudan, also rendered Khudun/Kudun) for a major left tributary of the Uda River in the Selenga basin.

b_saranka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; no pre-867 documentary record exists for a settlement or locality named Saranka in the Uda valley.
b_saranka.etymology_analysis: Russian-adapted Siberian botanical toponym from saranka ('Siberian martagon lily'), ultimately a Turkic loanword (sarana).

b_kansk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1628 CE as the Russian Cossack fort of Kansky ostrog (Канский острожек) on the Kan River, relocated to its current site in 1636 CE, and granted town status in 1782 CE.
b_kansk.etymology_analysis: Russian town name formed from the Kan River hydronym plus the Russian adjectival/settlement suffix -sk.

b_biriusa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian cartography and hydrological surveys as the 1,012 km Biryusa River in Irkutsk Oblast and Krasnoyarsk Krai.

morphemes.translation: river name (linked in local tradition to Evenki birosal, 'right bank')

b_biriusa.etymology_analysis: Siberian hydronym for the main western source river of the Taseyeva River, traditionally connected to Evenki birosal ('right bank').

b_khoidkhiliin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; no historical settlement or documented toponym of this name is recorded in the Kan-Yenisei basin.
b_khoidkhiliin.etymology_analysis: Mongolic compound meaning 'of the northern/rear border' (khoid + khil + -iin), unattested as a historical pre-867 settlement.

b_krasnoyarsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded on 19 August 1628 CE by Cossack voivode Andrey Dubensky as the Russian frontier fort of Krasny Yar ('Red Steep Bank'), calquing the local Turkic/Khakas name Kyzyl Char.
b_krasnoyarsk.etymology_analysis: Russian city name derived from Krasny Yar ('Red Steep Bank'), a calque of the indigenous Khakas/Turkic toponym Kyzyl Char, with the Russian urban suffix -sk.

b_kem_MON.first_mention_attestation: The hydronym Kem (Old Turkic Käm) for the Yenisei River system in southern/central Siberia is first attested in Chinese sources in the Book of Zhou (636 CE, vol. 50, as Jian Shui 劔水) and in the 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions (732/735 CE, as Käm).

morphemes.translation: great river (historical name for the Yenisei and its tributary)

b_kem_MON.etymology_analysis: Ancient Siberian hydronym (Old Turkic Käm, Tuvan khem 'river') attested since the 7th century CE for the Upper Yenisei and preserved in the Kem River tributary in Krasnoyarsk Krai.

b_kemchug.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrological surveys as the Kemchug River (Bolshoy and Maly Kemchug), a tributary of the Chulym in Krasnoyarsk Krai.
b_kemchug.etymology_analysis: Siberian hydronym combining the widespread regional river root kem ('river') with the suffix -chug.

b_stolby.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; Russian-named syenite rock formations (Stolby, 'Pillars') south of Krasnoyarsk, designated as the Stolby Nature Reserve in 1925 CE.
b_stolby.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive plural noun stolby ('pillars'), applied to the syenite rock formations near Krasnoyarsk.

b_mana_MON.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrological surveys as the 475 km Mana River, a right tributary of the Yenisei in Krasnoyarsk Krai.
b_mana_MON.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Siberian hydronym of pre-Russian origin for a right tributary of the Yenisei south of Krasnoyarsk.

b_kyzyl-kan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; no pre-867 documentary record exists for a settlement or locality named Kyzyl-Kan in the Mana-Kan basin.
b_kyzyl-kan.etymology_analysis: Turkic-Siberian compound combining kyzyl ('red') with the regional hydronym Kan.

b_shishina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrological registers as a 14 km right tributary of the Kan River in Krasnoyarsk Krai.
b_shishina.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for a small right tributary of the Kan River in Krasnoyarsk Krai, recorded in modern Russian river registers.

b_taseya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in Russian sources from the 17th century CE onward as the Taseyeva River (formed by the confluence of the Biryusa and Chuna).
b_taseya.etymology_analysis: Hydronym in Krasnoyarsk Krai formed in Russian from the name of the 17th-century local Tungus chieftain Tasey plus the possessive suffix -eva.

b_nemkina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrological registers as a 20 km left tributary of the Kan River in Krasnoyarsk Krai.
b_nemkina.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for a 20 km left tributary of the Kan River in Krasnoyarsk Krai, recorded in modern Russian river registers.

b_tagul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrological surveys as the Tagul River, a tributary of the Biryusa River in Irkutsk Oblast.
b_tagul.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Siberian hydronym for a tributary of the Biryusa River in the Eastern Sayan foothills.

b_agul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Russian hydrological surveys as the Agul River, a right tributary of the Kan River in Krasnoyarsk Krai.
b_agul.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Siberian hydronym for a right tributary of the Kan River flowing from the Eastern Sayan Mountains.

b_narsgol.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; no historical settlement or documented pre-867 toponym of this name is recorded in the Tagul-Kan basin.
b_narsgol.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Mongolian compound meaning 'Pine River' (nars + gol), unattested in pre-867 sources.

b_fic_mong_ulanhulud.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_ulanhulud); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_ulanhulud.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 Mongolic-style barony name formed with ulaan ('red').

b_fic_mong_tsagaanuur.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_tsagaanuur); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_tsagaanuur.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name from Mongolian tsagaan ('white') + nuur ('lake').

b_fic_mong_horobot.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_horobot); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_horobot.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name created for the eastern Gobi region.

b_mong_hepung.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; no historical settlement or locality named Hepung is documented in the eastern Gobi / Wuguguo region.
b_mong_hepung.etymology_analysis: CK3 barony name in the Wuguguo/eastern Gobi region with no pre-867 documentary attestation.

b_fic_mong_zovkerulen.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_zovkerulen); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_zovkerulen.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 directional/qualifier compound combining Mongolian zöv ('right/proper') with Kerülen (the Kherlen River).

b_fic_mong_kurnuur.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_kurnuur); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_kurnuur.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name from Mongolian khür ('brown/dark') + nuur ('lake').

b_fic_mong_khosoonuud.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_khosoonuud); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_khosoonuud.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name from Mongolian khoshoo ('monument/promontory') with plural suffix -nuud.

b_fic_mong_kanchuku.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_kanchuku); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_kanchuku.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name created for the eastern Gobi region.

b_fic_mong_usguitalbai.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_usguitalbai); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_usguitalbai.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name from Mongolian usgüi ('waterless') + talbai ('plain').

b_fic_mong_tapsunuur.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_tapsunuur); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_tapsunuur.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name from Mongolian davs ('salt') + nuur ('lake').

b_fic_mong_nuurkhoorond.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_nuurkhoorond); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_nuurkhoorond.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 locator compound from Mongolian nuur ('lake') + khoorond ('between').

b_fic_mong_tulanhara.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_tulanhara); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_tulanhara.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 Mongolic-style barony name incorporating Mongolian khar ('black').

b_fic_mong_khargobi.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (b_fic_mong_khargobi); does not correspond to a real-world settlement attested <= 867 CE.
b_fic_mong_khargobi.etymology_analysis: Synthetic CK3 barony name from Mongolian khar ('black') + govi ('arid desert/steppe').

b_gobi_kur_chagan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written or documentary sources <= 867 CE; no pre-867 settlement or locality named Kur Chagan is documented in the Gobi/Abaga region.
