b_gobi_dood_ongi.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Dood Ongi ('Lower Ongi') or the Ongi River (Ongi Gol).
b_gobi_dood_ongi.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound combining Mongolian dood ('lower') with Ongi (the Ongi River, Mongolian Ongi gol).

b_gobi_ochikhi.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Ochikhi (or the in-game county-seat fallback Ulaan Govi).
b_gobi_ochikhi.etymology_analysis: Mongolian Gobi barony Ochikhi (in-game county-seat fallback Ulângowi / Ulaan Govi, 'Red Gobi').

b_gobi_burgasutai.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Burgasutai.
b_gobi_burgasutai.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Mongolian toponym meaning 'having willows' (burgas + -tai), a common place-name in the Gobi region.

b_gobi_ulaan_nuur.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Ulaan Nuur (an endorheic lake in Ömnögovi Province fed by the Ongi River).
b_gobi_ulaan_nuur.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian ulaan ('red') and nuur ('lake'), referring to Ulaan Nuur in northern Ömnögovi Province.

b_gobi_bayanzag.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Flaming Cliffs (Bayanzag) gained international documentation during Roy Chapman Andrews's 1922–1925 American Museum of Natural History expeditions.
b_gobi_bayanzag.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian bayan ('rich') and zag ('saxaul tree'), meaning 'rich in saxaul', the Mongolian name for the Flaming Cliffs in Ömnögovi Province.

b_karabalgasun.first_mention_attestation: The Mongolian name Karabalgasun / Khar Balgas ('Black Ruins / Black City') is first recorded in modern travel accounts (e.g., Paderin in 1871) for the ruins of the Uyghur capital Ordu-Baliq (744–840 CE).
b_karabalgasun.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian khar ('black') and balgasun/balgas ('city, ruins'), applied after the city's 840 CE destruction to the ruins of Ordu-Baliq.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tamim ibn Bahr's 821 CE travel account and the early 9th-century Karabalgasun trilingual inscription (reign of Ay Tengride Qut Bulmish Alp Bilge Khagan, 808–821 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded c. 744 CE as the imperial capital of the Uyghur Khaganate under the Old Turkic name Ordu-Baliq ('royal camp city'); destroyed by the Yenisei Kyrgyz in 840 CE.

b_otuken_city.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Chinese dynastic histories (Zhou shu and Sui shu, completed 636 CE) as Yudujin/Dujin Mountain (於都斤山) and in the Old Turkic Orkhon inscriptions (Kul Tigin 732 CE, Bilge Khagan 735 CE) as Ötüken yïš ('Ötüken forest/mountain').
b_otuken_city.etymology_analysis: From Old Turkic Ötüken (Ötüken yïš / Ötüken jer), the sacred forested mountain homeland and imperial center of the Göktürk and Uyghur khaganates in central Mongolia.

b_hanhai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Sima Qian's Shiji (c. 91 BCE, ch. 111) recording Huo Qubing's 119 BCE campaign reaching Hanhai (翰海/瀚海), and later as the Tang Hanhai Protectorate (瀚海都護府, 663–669 CE).
b_hanhai.etymology_analysis: Classical Chinese choronym Hanhai ('Vast Sea'), denoting the Gobi desert and northern Mongolian steppe (and later the Tang Hanhai Protectorate).

b_sharga_OTU.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Sharga in the Orkhon region.
b_sharga_OTU.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian sharga ('dun, light bay/palomino'), a common descriptive toponym.

b_bulgan_uul.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Bulgan Uul.
b_bulgan_uul.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian bulgan ('sable') and uul ('mountain'), meaning 'Sable Mountain'.

b_karakorum.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1220 CE by Genghis Khan (attested in the Yuanshi and the 1342 Sino-Mongolian inscription of Karakorum) and walled in 1235 CE by Ögedei Khan.
b_karakorum.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian khar ('black') and khorum ('stone debris, boulder field'), referring to the nearby Kharkhorin mountains.

b_bayan_nuur.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Bayan Nuur.
b_bayan_nuur.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian bayan ('rich') and nuur ('lake'), meaning 'Rich Lake'.

b_longcheng.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Sima Qian's Shiji (c. 91 BCE, ch. 110) as Longcheng (蘢城/龍城), the seasonal assembly site and de facto capital of the Xiongnu Empire (c. 3rd century BCE–2nd century CE).
b_longcheng.etymology_analysis: Chinese name Longcheng (蘢城/龍城, 'Dragon City'; Mongolian Luut), the Xiongnu imperial assembly site in the Orkhon/Arkhangai region.

b_khogno_khan.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Khögnö Khan Mountain hosts the ruins of the 17th-century Erdene Khamba Monastery.
b_khogno_khan.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian khögnö ('tether-rope for lambs/kids') and khan ('lord/khan', an honorific for sacred mountains).

b_batkhaan.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Batkhaan Mountain (protected as a nature reserve since 1957/1974).
b_batkhaan.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian bat ('firm, strong') and khaan ('khan, sovereign'), a sacred mountain on the Töv–Övörkhangai border.

b_shankh.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Shankh Monastery was founded in 1647 CE by Zanabazar.
b_shankh.etymology_analysis: Mongolian name of Shankh Monastery (Shankh Khiid) and the adjacent locality near Kharkhorin; etymology uncertain (possibly a small mountain ridge or ordered group).

b_khanjargalant.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Khanjargalant.
b_khanjargalant.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian khan ('khan, sovereign') and jargalant ('blissful, prosperous').

b_ogiy.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Ögii Lake (Ögii Nuur) in Arkhangai Province.
b_ogiy.etymology_analysis: Mongolian hydronym Ögii (short for Ögii Nuur, a freshwater lake near the confluence of the Tamir and Orkhon rivers).

b_mumo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Liang shu (completed 636 CE) as Mumocheng (木末城), the early 6th-century CE capital of the Rouran Khaganate built c. 500–520 CE under Yujiulü Anagui.
b_mumo.etymology_analysis: From Chinese Mumocheng (木末城), transcribing the Rouran/Xianbei name Mumo for the 6th-century Rouran Khaganate capital.

b_khoyorgol.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Khoyor Gol.
b_khoyorgol.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian khoyor ('two') and gol ('river'), meaning 'Two Rivers'.

b_erdenet.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1974 CE as a planned mining city to exploit the Erdenetiin Ovoo copper-molybdenum deposit.
b_erdenet.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian erdene ('jewel, treasure') + possessive suffix -t, meaning 'having treasure / precious'.

b_ishgent.first_mention_attestation: No written documentary attestation <= 867 CE for Ishgent.
b_ishgent.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian ishig/ishgen ('kid, young goat') + possessive suffix -t, meaning 'having goat kids'.

b_FIC_Amur_Beihelin.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque) meaning 'North Helin' (北和林); no real-world settlement or written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Beihelin.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional compound combining Chinese bei ('north') with Helin (和林, short for Karakorum / Khara Khorin).

b_FIC_Amur_Humari.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque) corresponding to the Huma River (呼玛河 / 胡马日) in Heilongjiang; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Humari.etymology_analysis: Synthetic sinosphere_calque rendering of the Huma River (呼玛河, here written 胡马日), a tributary of the Amur River in northern Heilongjiang.

b_FIC_Mong_Banouhe.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 八弄河 'Eight-Defile River'); no real-world settlement or written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Mong_Banouhe.etymology_analysis: Synthetic Chinese hydronymic calque combining ba ('eight'), nong ('defile/alley'), and he ('river').

b_FIC_Amur_Jialingxi.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 假岭西 'Provisional West of the Ridge'); no real-world settlement or written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Jialingxi.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional/administrative compound combining Chinese jia ('provisional'), ling ('mountain ridge'), and xi ('west').

b_FIC_Amur_Yuancao.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 原草 'Plateau Grass'); no real-world settlement or written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Yuancao.etymology_analysis: Synthetic generic topographic compound combining Chinese yuan ('plain, plateau') and cao ('grass').

b_FIC_Amur_Hurka.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 呼日哈); in Tang/Bohai times the Mudan River was called Huhan (忽汗河), whereas the Jurchen name Hurka/Huligai (呼尔喀/胡里改) is post-867 (Jin/Yuan era).
b_FIC_Amur_Hurka.etymology_analysis: Synthetic sinosphere_calque rendering of Hurka (Jurchen/Manchu name for the Mudanjiang/Hurka River, here written 呼日哈).

b_FIC_Amur_Jiapowo.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 假婆莴); no real-world settlement or written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Jiapowo.etymology_analysis: Synthetic administrative compound combining Chinese jia ('provisional') with the county name Powo (婆莴).

b_FIC_Amur_Iskenhe.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 依西肯河) named after the Yixiken River/township in northern Heilongjiang; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Iskenhe.etymology_analysis: From the Tungusic/Oroqen hydronym Yixiken (依西肯) + Chinese he ('river').

b_FIC_Amur_Ganyijiang.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 甘夷江 'Sweet Eastern-Barbarian River'); no real-world settlement or written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Ganyijiang.etymology_analysis: Synthetic Chinese hydronymic compound combining gan ('sweet'), yi ('eastern peoples'), and jiang ('river').

b_FIC_Amur_Ganhejiang.first_mention_attestation: Synthetic CK3 barony (sinosphere_calque, 干河江) referencing the Gan River (甘河) in Hulunbuir, Inner Mongolia; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_FIC_Amur_Ganhejiang.etymology_analysis: Synthetic sinosphere_calque combining Ganhe (甘河/干河, Gan River in Inner Mongolia) with jiang ('river').
